name: Diego Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the office of a secondary school, about nine hundred kids. I'm the most junior of three admins, so I get attendance: chasing parents when a kid's absent, logging the late slips, booking supply teachers when someone's off sick. I also do a lot of filing, permission slips for trips, medical forms, that sort of thing. I'm still slow on the school's management system, Brenda who runs the office fixes my mistakes most weeks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rhythm of the school year, honestly, and the holidays help. I like the kids who come in with a note and a story about the bus. What wears me out is ringing parents at nine in the morning who swear at me because their kid's skipped again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, see, it was oversold, like a lot of things. In the staff room I'd say the AI thing that writes report comments was handy and that's about it. I'm not one for posting, but I'd maybe send a meme to the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means my job's fine. Schools change slowly, and parents still want a voice on the phone. The only thing on my mind would be the budget, because the head keeps saying money's tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd use the AI tool now and then for letters home, like I do now, because Brenda showed me and it's quicker. I'd keep saving for a deposit with Ana, my girlfriend, we've got about four months of bills put by and we want to buy in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, pretty much. A school's a steady place to be, the bells ring at the same time whatever happens with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the budget's tight. Could that touch your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if someone left they wouldn't replace them. But there's three of us and we're all busy, so I can't see them cutting one of us outright. I've seen the head fight to keep the office staff before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the deposit for, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A two-bed terrace near Ana's work, she's a dental nurse. We've been renting for three years, and the rent keeps creeping up. In this world we'd just keep chipping away at it.

say: I'd say AI was **oversold**, like a lot of things.
In the staff room I'd call the report-comment tool **handy**, nothing more.
think: My job's **fine**, because schools change slowly and parents want a voice.
The only worry is the **school budget**, which the head says is tight.
do: Keep using AI **now and then** for letters home, as Brenda showed me.
Keep saving for a **house deposit** with Ana, aiming to buy in two years.
feel: **Calm**, because a school feels like a **steady** place.
S0.quote: A school's a steady place to be, the bells ring at the same time whatever happens with AI.
fieldNote: He sees his job as **secure** because schools change slowly.
His main financial goal is a **house deposit** with his girlfriend.
Uses AI **occasionally**, only after a senior colleague showed him.

steps.text: Keep writing letters home with the AI tool now and then
Put a set amount into the house deposit each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say schools should use it carefully and keep people for the human stuff. I'd tell the other admins we'll be fine if we learn it. That's the sensible line, so that's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the attendance side is exactly the kind of thing software eats. Ringing parents, logging lates, booking supply teachers, a program could do all of that automatically. Our school's part of a group of five, and I've heard they want to centralise the admin, so I think the junior job goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Brenda to put me on the training for the new system as soon as it comes. I'd also start looking at teaching assistant jobs, because I like the kids and it's in the same building. And I'd put the house plan on hold for a year, so we're not stuck with a mortgage if I'm out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the system but also look at other jobs. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, to be honest. I'd learn the system because it might keep me in. But I'd have a backup, because I've seen how these things go, they say no one's losing their job and then they don't replace anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the deposit might take an extra year. She'd be disappointed, she's been looking at houses online every night. But she'd get it, her surgery's already using AI for bookings.

say: I'd say schools should keep people for the **human stuff**.
I'd tell the other admins we'll be fine if we **learn it**.
think: My **attendance work** is exactly what software eats.
The school group wants to **centralise admin**, so the junior job goes first.
do: Get on the **training** for the new system as soon as it arrives.
Look at **teaching assistant** jobs in the same building.
Put the **house plan** on hold for a year.
S1.quote: Ringing parents, logging lates, booking supply teachers, a program could do all of that automatically.
fieldNote: He spots that **attendance work** is easy to automate.

He hedges both ways: **learn the system** and line up a backup.

steps.text: Get trained on the school's new admin system
Apply for teaching assistant jobs at the school
Pause the house deposit plan for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and the government needs to step in, maybe a pause. I'm not a protester, but I'd tell people it's a big deal. In the staff room I'd say teachers need a plan too, not just us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the office job's gone by 2028. If AI can do any thinking work, it can run attendance and admissions and the whole lot. I'd still have a job for a bit if I got into the classroom, because looking after kids isn't just thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for a teaching assistant post straight away, even at less pay. I'd ask about the course to become a qualified assistant, the school pays for some of it. And we'd forget the house for now, keep renting, and keep the four months of savings as a buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the speed. Two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Teaching assistant pay is lower. Can you manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just. With Ana's wage we can cover the rent, but there'd be no extras. The holidays help, I could pick up summer work at the leisure centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when robots arrive in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what a robot does in a classroom. Maybe it marks things, maybe it watches the kids at lunch. I'd hope the parents still want a person there.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and the government should consider a **pause**.
In the staff room I'd say **teachers** need a plan too.
think: Getting into the **classroom** buys time, because caring for kids isn't just thinking.
do: Apply for a **teaching assistant** post straight away, even at less pay.
Drop the **house purchase** and keep renting.
S2.quote: If AI can do any thinking work, it can run attendance and admissions and the whole lot.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose** the office role and moves fast toward classroom work.
Lower pay is survivable only with **Ana's wage** and summer work.
Unsure what **robots** would do in schools, he hopes parents want people.

steps.text: Apply for a teaching assistant post at lower pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to sort it, so let's sort it. I'd tell the office we should all be learning the new systems. I'd say it calmly, because no one wants a scared admin on the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I can make the switch properly. I'd get the assistant qualification while still in the office, then move across. I'd be thirty-two by then, which is fine for a teaching assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the assistant course next September, evenings and some in-school days. I'd keep the office job for two years and use AI more, because Brenda would need help with the new tools. Then I'd move into the classroom full-time around 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but steadier. Like I've got a map, even if the road's bumpy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in year three, once I'm in the classroom. A small mortgage, nothing silly. Ana would want to, and I'd want her to have that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the parents who swear at you on the phone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, I'd say enjoy me while I'm here, the computer won't put up with you. Honestly though, I'd miss some of them. You get to know the regulars.

say: I'd say we've **got time** to sort it.
I'd tell the office we should all **learn the systems**, calmly.
think: Five years lets me make the **switch** to the classroom properly.
At **thirty-two**, starting as a teaching assistant is fine.
do: Keep the **office job** two years and use AI more.
S3.quote: Five years means I can make the switch properly.
fieldNote: Extra time turns his plan into a **timeline** he can name.
He'd help his senior colleague with **AI tools** before leaving.
House plans return later as a **small mortgage**.

steps.text: Start the teaching assistant course next September
Use AI tools to help with the office's new systems

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, schools will have it worked out. I'd tell people not to panic. I'd probably say it's like when computers came in, people adjusted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough that I might stay in the office a while longer. I'd move to the classroom eventually, but there's no rush. My worry is that I'd get comfortable and leave it too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the office job and get properly good at the new systems. In about three years I'd do the assistant course, and by year six I'd be in the classroom. We'd buy the house in the next couple of years, because there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious at the back of my mind, but mostly settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave it too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the money's fine and the holidays are good, why move? Being comfy is the trap. Brenda's lovely, too, which makes it worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you stop yourself falling into that trap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a date in the calendar. Literally, start the course by September 2029. Ana would hold me to it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years is nothing, and I'd be on lower pay with the house gone. What would help is the school paying for the assistant course and keeping people on while they train.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the kids think. They're growing up with this stuff. Some of the kids already ask me why I don't just use the computer for everything.

headlineQuote: Some of the kids already ask me why I don't just use the computer for everything.
portrait: Diego is the **junior admin** at a secondary school, handling attendance and filing.
He's **pragmatic**, likes the school year's rhythm, and is saving for a **house** with Ana.
He uses AI **occasionally**, after a senior colleague showed him.
His plan in every fast world is to move into the **classroom** as a teaching assistant.
His own risk, he says, is getting **comfortable** and leaving it late.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no room and the house goes.
whatWouldHelp: The school **funding the course** and keeping staff on during training.
